headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of COVID-19
headings.content: COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). First identified in late 2019, it quickly escalated into a global pandemic. Understanding its pathophysiology is crucial for nursing students in Nigeria and worldwide. SARS-CoV-2 is primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets and aerosols when an infected person coughs, sneezes, talks, or breathes. Once inside the human body, the virus utilizes its spike (S) glycoproteins to bind specifically to Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, which are abundantly expressed on the surface of human epithelial cells in the respiratory tract, vascular endothelium, heart, kidneys, and intestines. Following viral entry, viral replication triggers a localized immune response. In severe cases, this immune response becomes dysregulated, leading to a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, commonly referred to as a 'cytokine storm.' This hyperinflammatory state causes widespread endothelial injury, alveolar damage, microvascular thrombosis, and eventually acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), multi-organ failure, and death. Recognizing these mechanisms helps nurses appreciate why patients experience rapid clinical deterioration and multi-system involvement, guiding vigilant monitoring and timely interventions in clinical practice.

headings.title: Modes of Transmission and Infection Control Precautions
headings.content: Infection control is a cornerstone of nursing practice, particularly when managing highly transmissible respiratory pathogens like SARS-CoV-2. The virus spreads primarily through person-to-person contact via respiratory droplets and aerosols expelled during exhalation, speaking, coughing, or sneezing. Airborne transmission can also occur in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces during aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) such as intubation, suctioning, or nebulizer therapy. To protect healthcare workers, patients, and the wider community, strict infection control precautions must be implemented in all healthcare facilities across Nigeria. Standard precautions, including rigorous hand hygiene with soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub, must be practiced for every patient encounter. Transmission-based precautions are equally vital: healthcare personnel caring for suspected or confirmed COVID-19 patients must utilize appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), which includes medical masks or N95/FFP2 respirators, eye protection (goggles or face shields), gowns, and gloves. Airborne precautions are mandatory during AGPs. Furthermore, environmental controls such as ensuring adequate room ventilation, cohorting infected patients, and enforcing strict visitor restrictions play a significant role in interrupting the chain of transmission within clinical settings.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Severity Classification
headings.content: COVID-19 presents with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from entirely asymptomatic infection to critical illness and death. The incubation period typically ranges from 2 to 14 days. Common symptoms include fever or chills, cough, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, new loss of taste or smell, sore throat, congestion or runny nose, nausea or vomiting, and diarrhea. To guide clinical management and resource allocation, the World Health Organization and national guidelines classify COVID-19 severity into distinct categories: asymptomatic, mild, moderate, severe, and critical. Mild illness is characterized by various symptoms without signs of breathlessness or abnormal imaging. Moderate illness involves clinical or imaging evidence of lower respiratory disease with an oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 93% or higher on room air at sea level. Severe illness presents with clinical signs of pneumonia plus an SpO2 of less than 93% on room air, a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths per minute, or lung infiltrates exceeding 50%. Critical illness is defined by the presence of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), septic shock, and/or multiple organ dysfunction requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Nurses must master these classifications to quickly triage patients and escalate care appropriately.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Findings
headings.content: Accurate diagnostic evaluation is essential for confirming SARS-CoV-2 infection, assessing disease severity, and monitoring patient progress. The gold standard for direct viral detection is the Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) test, performed on upper respiratory specimens such as nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal swabs. RT-PCR detects viral RNA with high sensitivity and specificity. Rapid Antigen Detection Tests (RATs) offer quicker results at the point of care, though they generally possess lower sensitivity than RT-PCR. In addition to virological testing, laboratory findings provide critical insights into the patient's systemic status. Common hematological and biochemical abnormalities in moderate to severe COVID-19 include lymphopenia (low lymphocyte count), elevated inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), ferritin, and procalcitonin (which may indicate secondary bacterial infection). Coagulation profiles often show elevated D-dimer and fibrinogen levels, reflecting a hypercoagulable state and a high risk for thrombotic events. Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs) reveal hypoxemia and acid-base disturbances in respiratory failure. Imaging studies, including chest radiography and computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest, frequently demonstrate bilateral ground-glass opacities and patchy consolidations. Nurses must collaborate with the laboratory and radiology teams to ensure prompt collection, safe handling, and accurate interpretation of these diagnostics.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Monitoring of COVID-19 Patients
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment and continuous monitoring are vital for detecting early signs of clinical deterioration in COVID-19 patients. Nurses must perform frequent head-to-toe assessments, placing special emphasis on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. Vital signs, particularly oxygen saturation via pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature, should be monitored routinely according to the patient's acuity level. Nurses must watch closely for 'happy hypoxemia'—a phenomenon where patients exhibit dangerously low oxygen saturation levels without reporting severe shortness of breath. Assessing the work of breathing is crucial; nurses should observe for the use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and tachypnea. Regular neurological checks are necessary to assess for confusion, lethargy, or altered mental status, which often signal cerebral hypoxia or severe systemic inflammation. Fluid balance charting is essential, requiring precise measurement of intake and output to prevent both fluid overload and dehydration, especially in febrile patients or those receiving mechanical ventilation. Furthermore, monitoring peripheral perfusion, skin integrity (to prevent pressure injuries during prolonged prone positioning), and emotional well-being forms a holistic part of the nursing care plan.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of COVID-19 has evolved significantly, tailored to the stage of the disease and its severity. Treatment protocols generally divide care into antiviral therapy for early, mild-to-moderate disease and immunomodulatory therapy for severe, hyperinflammatory states. Antiviral medications, such as nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) or remdesivir, work by inhibiting viral replication and are most effective when administered early in the course of infection for patients at high risk of progression. For hospitalized patients requiring supplemental oxygen, anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agents are standard. Corticosteroids, specifically dexamethasone, are proven to reduce mortality in patients requiring oxygen support by dampening the destructive systemic immune response. Additional immunomodulators, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonists (e.g., tocilizumab) or Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (e.g., baricitinib), may be added for patients experiencing rapid respiratory deterioration and severe systemic inflammation. Thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is routinely prescribed to mitigate the high risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pulmonary embolism associated with COVID-19. Nurses play a critical role in administering these medications safely, monitoring for adverse drug reactions, checking renal and hepatic function parameters, and evaluating therapeutic efficacy.

headings.title: Respiratory Support and Oxygen Therapy
headings.content: Respiratory support is the cornerstone of managing moderate to critical COVID-19 patients. When hypoxemia develops, prompt initiation of oxygen therapy is required to maintain adequate tissue oxygenation (typically targeting an SpO2 of 92-96% for most patients, or 88-92% for those with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure). Initial support often begins with low-flow nasal cannulas or simple face masks. For patients with higher oxygen requirements, high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy provides heated and humidified oxygen at high flow rates, reducing the need for invasive mechanical ventilation and improving patient comfort. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV), such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), can also be utilized, though close monitoring is necessary to avoid delayed intubation. When respiratory failure progresses and non-invasive methods fail, endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation become mandatory. In ventilated patients with refractory hypoxemia, proning—placing the patient in a prone (belly-down) position for 12 to 16 hours a day—is a vital intervention that improves ventilation-perfusion matching and lung recruitment. Nurses caring for patients receiving respiratory support must manage equipment, monitor circuit integrity, provide meticulous airway care, and perform frequent respiratory assessments.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Long COVID
headings.content: While many individuals recover fully from COVID-19, others experience severe acute complications and persistent long-term health issues. Acute complications during the illness include acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), secondary bacterial infections (such as ventilator-associated pneumonia), sepsis, acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy, cardiac arrhythmias, myocarditis, and thromboembolic events like deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Furthermore, a significant number of survivors experience 'Long COVID' or post-COVID-19 condition, characterized by symptoms that persist or develop weeks to months after the acute infection has resolved. Common long COVID symptoms include profound fatigue, shortness of breath, 'brain fog' (cognitive impairment), sleep disturbances, joint pain, persistent cough, anxiety, and depression. The exact pathophysiology of long COVID is still under investigation, with theories suggesting persistent viral reservoirs, chronic low-grade inflammation, and autoimmunity. Nurses caring for these patients must provide comprehensive, compassionate care, recognizing the multi-system nature of long COVID and facilitating referrals to multidisciplinary rehabilitation programs focusing on physical therapy, psychological support, and nutritional counseling.

headings.title: Patient Education and Public Health Prevention
headings.content: Patient education and public health prevention are vital components of nursing practice aimed at halting the spread of COVID-19 and empowering communities. Nurses serve as trusted educators, translating complex scientific data into clear, actionable advice for patients and the public. Key preventive measures include promoting widespread vaccination, which remains the most effective defense against severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. Nurses must educate communities about vaccine safety, efficacy, and the importance of completing recommended booster doses. Additional public health education emphasizes correct and consistent mask-wearing in crowded or indoor settings, practicing diligent hand hygiene with soap and water or alcohol-based hand sanitizer, maintaining physical distancing, and ensuring adequate indoor ventilation. Nurses should also advise individuals who test positive or have been exposed to isolate or quarantine according to current public health guidelines to prevent community spread. Empowering patients with knowledge regarding symptom self-monitoring, when to seek emergency medical attention (such as sudden chest pain or severe difficulty breathing), and debunking health misinformation are crucial nursing responsibilities that foster community resilience and health literacy.
